newsitem.title: UK: Rain seen cutting E Europe grain exports.
newsitem.headline: Rain seen cutting E Europe grain exports.

text.p: Rain could force analysts to revise down ideas on exports from eastern Europe's big grain producers, Romania and Hungary, according to London based trade sources.

Although those countries have not been the worst hit by recent flooding in Eastern Europe, wet weather has hit quality and looks likely to up the proportion of feed wheat in the crop, western European analysts said.

According to the International Grains Council, Hungary will export 1.5 million tonnes of wheat in 1997-98 (July-June), while Romania is on its way to turn in a massively increased crop into exports of 1.3 million.
But these estimates were published at the start of the month and some analysts see the figures coming down when the IGC publishes new estimates on Thursday.
Poland, the Czech Republic and Slovakia and eastern parts of Germany have been worst hit by flooding, but the areas directly affected are of limited importance in terms of grain production.
Crops in Hungary and Romania still look good in yield terms, western analysts said. But they are concerned over the effect of widespread rain on quality.

Romanian government officials have denied suggestions that adverse weather which has hit other parts of eastern Europe could adversely affect the crop. They described it as excellent, with more than 40 percent harvested and initial yields exceeding officials estimates. Romania's wheat crop is expected to more than double to 7.07 million tonnes, with exports seen at over two million tonnes, according to the ministry of agriculture.
"The volume produced in Romania may not be as high as some of the forecasts, but it's still going to be way up on last year," one authoritative London based analyst said.
IGC figures put the 1996 Romanian crop at 3.2 million tonnes, while the IGC's most recent estimate for Romanian production in 1997 is 7.8 million.
For Hungary he was more concerned over quality than quantity. "They were looking for a good quality crop, but now it looks as though they are going to have a lot of feed wheat," he said.
Hungary's harvest has been slowed by wet weather, cutting the likely proportion of milling wheat and forcing up the price premium for milling over feed wheat.
IGC estimates show a five million tonne wheat crop in Hungary this year, up from 3.9 million in 1996.

The flooding was expected to hit Poland's rapeseed crop. According to Hamburg based newsletter Oil World, Poland's 1997 rapeseed crop could fall to 350,000 tonnes from 461,000 last year and the 906,000 tonne average recorded between 1991 and 1995.
"They were hit by winterkill last year and they've got the floods this year," one London based analyst said.
"They were just ready for harvesting when the rain started." --Christopher Lyddon, London newsroom +44 171 542 7928
